summaries.example: Imagine a robot that follows written instructions to sort cards. If the instructions always eventually tell the robot to stop and give the right answer, that task is computable. But some instructions may make the robot repeat steps forever. There is no single method that can correctly predict, for every possible program and input, whether it will stop.
summaries.summary:
Computability is about what can be solved by following exact instructions. Before modern computers existed, thinkers such as Gödel, Church, and Turing developed different precise models of calculation. These models were surprisingly equivalent: anything computable in one could be computed in the others. This idea is connected with the Church–Turing thesis, which says that these models capture what it means to be computable in principle.

Turing machines are very simple imaginary machines. They have a tape for storing symbols, a head that reads and writes one symbol at a time, and rules for moving and changing state. A universal Turing machine can follow the instructions of any other Turing machine. This is the basic idea behind a general-purpose computer: one device can run many different programs.

Some machines never stop on certain inputs. The halting problem asks whether there can be one method that always predicts which programs will stop. Turing showed that no such method can work for every program and input. A problem may still be listable or recognizable: a machine might eventually confirm “yes” when the answer is yes, while running forever when the answer is no. A decidable problem is stronger: a machine always stops and says yes or no.

The entry also studies complexity. Two problems may both be computable, but one may need much more time or memory. Complexity classes, including P and NP, help compare these resources and show why some useful-looking problems are difficult in practice.
key_ideas: Many different mathematical models of computation turn out to have the same basic power.
A universal machine can use different instructions to perform many different tasks.
Some tasks are computable in principle, but some are not.
A general test for whether every program will stop is impossible.
Complexity asks not only whether a task can be solved, but whether it can be solved fast enough to be useful.
The class P is used as a mathematical guide to problems that often have efficient solutions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Computability helps us understand the limits of programs and machines. It explains why some questions cannot be answered by an automatic method that works in every case. Complexity helps us understand why a solvable problem may still be too slow for practical use. Together, these ideas guide computer science and sharpen questions about what machines can and cannot do.

summaries.example: Consider a program that receives another program and its input, then tries to announce whether that program will eventually stop. If such a predictor existed for every program, one could construct a program that does the opposite of the predictor’s answer when given its own description. If the predictor says the constructed program stops, it loops; if the predictor says it loops, it stops. The contradiction shows that no universal halting predictor can exist.
summaries.summary:
The entry distinguishes two questions: what can be computed at all, and what can be computed with acceptable resources. In the 1930s, several formal systems were proposed to capture effective calculation, including Turing machines, lambda calculus, recursive functions, and other symbolic systems. Their equivalence was striking: each can compute exactly what the others can compute. The Church–Turing thesis identifies this shared formal notion with computation in principle, although the thesis is an explanatory claim about an informal concept.

A Turing machine has finitely many internal states, a tape that can provide unbounded workspace, a read/write head, and a transition rule. Its description is a finite string, so descriptions can themselves be treated as inputs. Turing’s universal machine uses one encoded description to simulate the corresponding machine on an input. This gives a conceptual basis for general-purpose computers.

Because machines can loop, computability must distinguish partial from total behavior. A machine may compute an output on some inputs and remain undefined on others because it never halts. A recursively enumerable set can be listed by a machine, or accepted by a machine that eventually halts on members; it need not provide a terminating answer for nonmembers. A decidable set has a total procedure that halts with the correct yes-or-no answer. A set is decidable exactly when both it and its complement are recursively enumerable.

The halting problem asks whether there is a procedure that decides, for every machine and input, whether the machine eventually halts. Turing’s diagonal construction shows that there is not. key_ideas: Formal models developed independently by Church, Gödel, Turing, and others were shown to compute the same class of functions.
The Church–Turing thesis connects this formal agreement with the informal idea of computation in principle; it is a thesis about the adequacy of the models, not merely a definition.
A universal machine separates hardware from instructions: one machine can simulate any encoded machine.
Recursively enumerable problems need not be decidable, because a computation may confirm positive cases while never halting on negative cases.
Diagonal reasoning establishes that the halting problem is undecidable and that no total candidate class can capture every computable function without an operation such as unbounded search.

Complexity theory restricts attention to computations that halt and compares their worst-case resource use; P, NP, PSPACE, and EXPTIME form a known chain of inclusions, though several strictness questions remain open.
summaries.why_it_matters:
Computability theory places principled limits on automation. It shows that failure to find an algorithm is not always a temporary engineering problem: some problems admit no algorithm that always returns the right answer. The distinction between enumeration, acceptance, and decision also clarifies what a program can establish when it may fail to halt.

Complexity theory adds a different kind of limit. It assumes total computations and measures worst-case time or memory as a function of input length. summaries.example: Suppose you are designing a game with a program that searches through possible moves. For some starting positions, it finds an answer and stops. For others, it may keep searching forever. You might try to build a second program that predicts whether the first one will stop. The halting problem shows that no prediction program can succeed for every possible program and starting position.
summaries.summary:
Computability asks what can be done by a precise procedure. Before electronic computers, mathematicians proposed several formal models, such as Turing machines, lambda calculus, and recursive functions. They discovered that these models have the same computing power. This agreement supports the Church–Turing thesis: the formal idea of computation captures the ordinary idea of carrying out a calculation by definite rules.

A Turing machine is deliberately simple. It has a finite collection of states, a tape with symbols, a head that reads and writes, and a rule telling it what to do next. The tape can be as long as needed, although the head changes only a small amount of information at each step. A universal machine can read an encoded program for another machine and simulate it. Thus a single general machine can perform many tasks.

This power has a limit. Some machines never halt on some inputs. The halting problem asks whether an algorithm could always determine in advance whether any given machine and input will eventually stop. Turing’s diagonal argument shows that it cannot. The argument uses self-reference: a supposed perfect predictor can be used to make a machine that behaves opposite to the prediction about itself.

The entry distinguishes recursively enumerable sets from decidable sets. A recursively enumerable set can be produced by a machine or recognized when a positive case eventually appears, but the machine may run forever for a negative case. A decidable set has a procedure that halts for every input and answers both possibilities. The entry also discusses primitive recursive and recursive functions, showing how different definitions of computability relate.

key_ideas: Different formal descriptions of computation, including Turing machines and lambda calculus, have been shown to be equivalent in what they can compute.
The Church–Turing thesis says these formal descriptions match the ordinary idea of a calculation that can be carried out by definite steps.
A universal machine shows how one general machine can run many different programs.
A program may confirm that an item belongs to a set without ever confirming that it does not belong.
The halting problem is not decidable, so some limits on algorithms are mathematical rather than technological.
Complexity studies the resources needed for solvable problems, and the relationships among P, NP, PSPACE, and EXPTIME are not all settled.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas help separate three claims that are easy to confuse: a problem may be solvable in principle, recognizable only in positive cases, or solvable quickly enough to be useful. Computability theory identifies tasks that no universal algorithm can complete. Complexity theory helps explain why other tasks, though solvable, may require too much time or memory. This distinction matters whenever we judge what computers, software, or mathematical methods can accomplish.

A way to measure the time or memory needed as the size of a problem grows.
A class of problems solvable in polynomial time; it is often used as a mathematical approximation of feasible problems.
